newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FERC approves electricity path tracking test.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FERC approves electricity path tracking test.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Tuesday approved a two-year test of a system to track the paths taken by electricity over the power grid from generators to customers.
The aim of the test is to see if transmission rates can be based on the actual paths taken by electrons.

Under existing rules, rates are based on paths named in contracts which do not necessarily reflect the actual flow of electrons through the grid. So utilities whose wires are carrying electrons from other power producers are not necessarily being paid for the use of their lines.

In the experiment, called the General Agreement on Power Paths, participating utilities will be paid for carrying power based on the way electricity flows, a system that consumer advocates are seeking in federal power legislation.
Computers will be used to track the flow of electricity, which will then be posted on computers to all participants in the pilot program.
It will be up to power providers in the program to decide if they want to take service from the transmission owners to which they are referred.
If they do opt to use a new contract path, utility transmission owners will share their revenues with any transmission owners on the new path which carry at least five percent of the power flow.

Participants in the GAPP program are the public utility operating companies owned by Allegheny Power System ; Centerior Energy Corp subsidiaries Cleveland Electric Illuminating Co and Toledo Edison Co; Ohio Edison Co and its subsidiary Pennsylvania Power Co; Southern Co Services Inc and its utility subsidiaries; Virginia Electric and Power Co ; and Ontario Hydro.
